item.title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Ab initio construction of order n=8 Trotter-Suzuki product formulas, yielding more efficient compositions and the first generic schemes (q≥27 cycles). With ZNE mitigation at two-qubit depolarizing rate p2q=10−5, the n=8 scheme reaches minimal infidelity 0.0034% versus 0.034% for second-order Leapfrog.

Grade 0.413 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Marko Malevzivc, Johann Ostmeyer

Figure

Experimental error Errnexp. versus computational cost q/h for global and local operator groupings on an L=6 Heisenberg XZ chain. The author's recommended q=21 composition and q=30 generic schemes consistently outperform the baseline schemes by Morales et al.

Asks

Can Omelyan's direct error-term optimization approach be extended to order n=8 to derive more efficient Trotter decompositions than existing compositions of second-order schemes?

Before

Morales et al. composition schemes at order n=8.

But

Simulated quantum circuits; evaluated on 1D open-boundary Heisenberg XZ spin chains (L=6); depolarizing noise model.

Tools

Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion · free Lie algebra commutator basis · pybch · constrained numerical optimization · qiskit-omelyan

Abstract

Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order n could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond 6^th order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to 6^th order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order n = 8, and find both more efficient compositions and the first 8^th order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

item.title: Scheduling the quantum implementation of the Trotter decomposition for Hamiltonian simulation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Cyclic-2 scheduling combining simultaneous diagonalization with traveling-salesman cell CNOT optimization achieves second-order O(t3/r2) Trotter error scaling while preserving first-order sub-unitary count Lr. For a dihydrogen molecular Hamiltonian, it reaches target precision at circuit depth ~200 where prior strategies require depth >1000.

Grade 0.385 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Augustin Ho (Graduate School of Science and Technology, Keio University, École des Mines de Saint-Étienne), Naoki Yamamoto (Graduate School of Science and Technology, Keio University, Quantum Computing Center, Keio University)

Figure

Error versus circuit depth and Trotter step r for dihydrogen simulation (t=3). Shows cyclic-2 surpassing DepleteGroups for r>3 and matching precision at circuit depth ~200 that requires depth >1000 for static baselines.

Asks

How can the execution order of sub-Hamiltonians in Trotter decomposition be scheduled to simultaneously reduce both algorithmic error and circuit depth without increasing sub-unitary count?

Before

Simultaneous diagonalization, MaxCommuteTSP, and molecular-specific DepleteGroups (all static first-order orderings requiring depth >1000 for the precision cyclic-2 hits at depth ~200 on dihydrogen).

But

Classical simulations only; tested on systems up to n=8 qubits; fourth-order cyclic-10 shows no benefit over cyclic-2 for r≤20 Trotter steps; small circuit depth disadvantage observed for 8-qubit Heisenberg model versus standard simultaneous diagonalization.

Tools

Cyclic-2 alternating forward-backward Trotter scheduling · Simultaneous diagonalization via graph coloring · Cell CNOT optimization via Traveling Salesman Problem heuristics · OpenFermion simulation package

Abstract

For the quantum computational task for Hamiltonian simulation, the arrangement in which sub-Hamiltonians appear in the Trotter decomposition may have a large influence on the precision, under a given circuit complexity. In this paper, we design several scheduling strategies by combining two methods; that is, the existing simultaneous diagonalization scheme leveraged in order to guarantee the performance in a relatively short circuit depth, with a method inspired from a Trotter-Suzuki decomposition of the second or the fourth order for a better accuracy. By conducting numerical simulations on various Hamiltonian instances, we confirm a systematic advantage over previous methods. Thus, our proposal may eliminate the need of dealing with several Hamiltonian-dependent scheduling strategies.

item.title: Ancilla-Free Exact Dicke-State Synthesis with Optimal Size and Depth
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Every n-qubit Dicke state |Dkn⟩ can be prepared exactly without ancillary qubits in O(log⁡n) circuit depth using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs.

Grade 0.364 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Yunqi Huang, Wei Zi, Jianhao He, Zekun Ye, Shenggen Zheng

Figure

Schematic of the ancilla-free circuit architecture: coherent compression of 31-qubit blocks into 5 qubits releases 26 ancilla qubits to compute total weight and apply phase operations, which drive constant-step exact amplitude amplification.

Asks

Can every n-qubit Dicke state be prepared exactly using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs, with O(log⁡n) depth and without ancillary qubits?

Before

For balanced Dicke states, exact ancilla-free circuits required O(n2) gates and O(n) depth (Bärtschi and Eidenbenz 2019, Yuan and Zhang 2025). Polylogarithmic depth required O(nlog⁡n) ancillary qubits (Liu, Childs, and Gottesman 2024).

But

Asymptotic scaling in the circuit model with arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs; holds for any n≥2 and 1≤k≤n−1.

Tools

coherent block compression · reversible carry-save addition · weight-dependent phase correction · exact amplitude amplification

Abstract

We construct exact circuits for n-qubit Dicke states of any Hamming weight k using O(n) single-qubit gates and CNOTs in O(logn) depth without ancillary qubits. The gate count and depth are asymptotically optimal for every 0<k<n. We compress symmetric blocks to free output qubits for weight-dependent phases. A sign correction followed by a collective rotation produces a state whose overlap with the target is at least a positive constant, so exact amplitude amplification takes O(1) steps. For balanced Dicke states (k=lfloorn/2rfloor), the logarithmic depth disproves the Ω(k) depth lower bound conjectured by Yuan and Zhang (2025).

item.title: Quantum computing for gearing down complex many-fermion problems
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Joint simulated-annealing search over natural-orbital transformations and active-space selections reproduces exact ground-state energies and angular momenta J for 19O and 21O using |A|=11 active orbitals instead of the full sd space of Nsp=12.

Grade 0.362 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Weijie Du, Filippo Fornetti, James P. Vary

Figure

Ground-state energy and absolute error $|Δ E|$ and $|Δ J|$ versus active-space size |A| for 19O and 21O, comparing the hybrid quantum-classical search against exact full-space and bare-truncation calculations.

Asks

How can complex many-fermion ab initio problems beyond classical limits be mapped onto compact single-particle bases suitable for classical solvers using low-depth quantum circuits?

But

Demonstrated only on a valence-neutron shell-model model space with Nsp=12 under noiseless classical quantum circuit simulation.

Tools

Simulated annealing · Natural orbitals (NOs) · Block-encoded Hamiltonian sampling · Configuration interaction (CI) · Qiskit noiseless statevector simulation

Abstract

Quantum computing unlocks exciting opportunities to extend first-principles calculations of quantum many-body systems beyond classical computing limits. Despite advances in algorithms and proof-of-principle experiments, large-scale ab initio calculations on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain challenging. We introduce a quantum-classical framework that identifies compact single-particle bases to bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach while preserving an accurate ground-state description. We develop an efficient adaptive search scheme driven by simulated annealing that jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. A quantum-assisted ground-state estimator provides search guidance using low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements, making the framework promising for NISQ devices. We demonstrate the framework's applicability for the nuclear structure of the oxygen isotopes. Our framework opens a new route to tackling complex ab initio many-fermion problems across disciplines through quantum-assisted basis reduction.

item.title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Discretized Riemannian gradient flow compiled into quantum circuits optimizes models directly within the quantum domain without classical feedback or measurements, decreasing training loss exponentially with iterations for sufficiently small step sizes and bounding generalization error by 𝒪((deff2log⁡(deffN)+log⁡(1/δ))/N).

Grade 0.360 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Kasidit Srimahajariyapong, Thiparat Chotibut, Suwannachad Suwannajitt, Tithivich Paka, Ricard Puig, Yudai Suzuki, Marek Gluza, Zoë Holmes, Supanut Thanasilp

Figure

Training loss, testing loss, and infidelity plotted against iterations (with N=20) and sample size N for learning an n=8 qubit unitary, demonstrating rapid convergence and symmetry inheritance with few training states.

Asks

Can classical optimizers and intermediate quantum-to-classical measurements be completely eliminated from quantum machine learning training loops?

But

Circuit depth grows exponentially in training iterations with dataset size as the base of the exponent. Autonomous execution requires loss functions where gradient updates avoid evaluating intermediate expectations.

Tools

Riemannian gradient optimization · unitary Lie algebra bracket compilation · state 2-design analysis · covering net volumetric bounds

Abstract

Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without a priori specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

item.title: Tackling Many-Body Coulomb Singularity by Randomization
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Supersmoothing qDRIFT achieves diamond-norm error ‖Φ−𝒰T‖⋄≤CL(c02N4T+c04N8T2) for many-body Coulomb dynamics. Convergence is first-order in step size uniformly over all L2(ℝ3N) initial states without domain, smoothness, or energy restrictions.

Grade 0.353 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Di Fang, Wook Yoon

Figure

Full two-body trace-norm error versus number of time steps L at T=1 for hydrogen ground-state dynamics. Lie-Trotter, Strang, 4th-order Suzuki, and conventional qDRIFT stagnate near L−3/4 scaling, while supersmoothing qDRIFT surpasses L−1 scaling.

Asks

How can continuum many-body Coulomb dynamics be simulated efficiently on a quantum computer despite singular interactions and an unbounded Hamiltonian?

Before

Standard Trotter and conventional qDRIFT exhibit order reduction to t5/4 or slower local rates on hydrogen-like states, decaying as slowly as 1/log⁡L for general L2 initial states and bounded by L−3/4 for H2 initial states under conventional qDRIFT.

But

First-order in time. Asymptotic end-to-end gate bound 𝒪~(T2N7/ϵ) assumes charged particles with mass ratios bounded away from zero.

Tools

supersmoothing qDRIFT · Kato supersmoothing · randomized interaction kick times · spatial discretization analysis

Abstract

Many-body Coulomb dynamics is central to quantum chemistry and molecular simulation, yet the Coulomb singularity undermines both the standard error analysis and performance of product formulas. Even for the simple hydrogen ground state, the celebrated Trotter formulas converge more slowly than their nominal order, and going to higher order does not help. Randomization by itself does not resolve this. We show that conventional qDRIFT suffers the same loss of accuracy, and that for general initial states, the errors of both Trotter formulas and qDRIFT can decrease more slowly than any power of the number of time steps (logarithmically). To overcome these limitations, we introduce supersmoothing qDRIFT, a randomized product formula that turns a physical property of free particle propagation into an algorithmic resource. Our algorithm achieves an error bound that decreases linearly with the time step, uniformly over all initial states and without any smoothness or energy assumptions. Combined with spatial discretization analysis, the resulting end-to-end gate count improves on those of qubitization and high-order Trotter formulas applied directly to the discretized Hamiltonian, despite first-order convergence in time. This work demonstrates new ways of utilizing continuum dynamics to achieve algorithmic advantage.

item.arxave:abstract: Many-body Coulomb dynamics is central to quantum chemistry and molecular simulation, yet the Coulomb singularity undermines both the standard error analysis and performance of product formulas. Even for the simple hydrogen ground state, the celebrated Trotter formulas converge more slowly than their nominal order, and going to higher order does not help. Randomization by itself does not resolve this. We show that conventional qDRIFT suffers the same loss of accuracy, and that for general initial states, the errors of both Trotter formulas and qDRIFT can decrease more slowly than any power of the number of time steps (logarithmically). To overcome these limitations, we introduce supersmoothing qDRIFT, a randomized product formula that turns a physical property of free particle propagation into an algorithmic resource. Our algorithm achieves an error bound that decreases linearly with the time step, uniformly over all initial states and without any smoothness or energy assumptions. Combined with spatial discretization analysis, the resulting end-to-end gate count improves on those of qubitization and high-order Trotter formulas applied directly to the discretized Hamiltonian, despite first-order convergence in time. This work demonstrates new ways of utilizing continuum dynamics to achieve algorithmic advantage.

item.title: Efficient Tensor Decomposition of the Coulomb and Coulomb-like Potentials and Its Application to Probing Molecular Geometries Using a Quantum Computer
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Canonical polyadic decomposition of real-space grid Coulomb potentials achieves 𝒪(N1/3) T-gate scaling per Coulomb term with rank 8, yielding hydrogen atom energies to ∼10−5 Hartree precision at grid spacing Δx=0.6 Bohr.

Grade 0.343 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · James Brown, Masashi Takahashi, Robert Wodraszka, James Whitfield

Figure

T-gate count plotted against grid dimension N1/3 for a single application of the decomposed one-body Coulomb operator, verifying the 𝒪(N1/3) scaling.

Asks

Can real-space Coulomb potentials in first-quantized grid representations be efficiently decomposed to reduce block-encoding circuit complexity and T-gate scaling on quantum computers?

Before

Tensor hypercontraction and quadrature-based CP representations had required ranks of 15 to roughly 50 to represent Coulomb interactions.

But

Numerical tests limited to single hydrogen, helium, LiH, and a 1D single-particle pseudo-Coulomb model; neglects two-body Toeplitz optimisations.

Tools

canonical polyadic decomposition · alternating least squares · discrete variable representation · Chebyshev spectral filtering · Qualtran resource estimation

Abstract

We present an efficient canonical polyadic decomposition of the Coulomb and Coulomb-like potentials in real-space grid representations suited to quantum computing applications. By decomposing the matrix elements of Coulomb-like potentials into low-rank Cartesian components, we achieve O(N^(1/3)) T-gate scaling per Coulomb term, where N is the number of grid points (basis functions) per electron, while maintaining high accuracy. This opens a path to significantly reducing the number of basis functions (i.e., qubits) required compared to previous methods by utilizing improved representations of the Coulomb potential that converge faster with grid spacing. The decomposition is also valid for certain pseudopotentials, which can decrease the cost significantly compared to previous work. This efficient decomposition enables the application of block-encoding techniques at larger grid spacings than with previous decompositions, and can therefore be used for algorithms that do not require high energy accuracy. We apply this decomposed Coulomb potential to hydrogen atom energy levels, the helium ground-state energy, and the Hartree-Fock potential energy curve of LiH, and show that modest basis sizes achieve semi-quantitative to quantitative accuracy. As an example of where these faster-converging Coulomb representations can be used on a quantum computer, we discuss their application to probing low-energy molecular geometries, and we estimate the resulting reduction in the cost of real-time evolution.

item.title: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization benchmark problems from mixed Hamming packings
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Mixed Hamming packing yields a 133-instance QUBO benchmark suite (5 to 1325 variables, densities 8% to 100%) occupying a distinct region in MQLib feature space. Densely connected antiferromagnetic couplings nearly cancel local fields, leaving narrow energy margins that defeat D-Wave quantum annealers across all tested annealing times.

Grade 0.341 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Péter Naszvadi, Marcell Tukora, Roman Kuvzel, Mátyás Koniorczyk

Figure

Projection of QUBO benchmark sets onto the first two principal components of graph-theoretic features. The proposed Hamming packing instances cluster in an unoccupied feature space distinct from MQLib and existing quantum benchmarks.

Asks

Can realistic application problems from coding theory provide small yet challenging QUBO benchmarks that systematically differ from existing quantum-oriented benchmarks?

Before

Existing quantum-oriented benchmarks (tile-planting, heavy-hex instances) lie along a narrow, sparse border of the MQLib feature space, leaving the region occupied by these packing instances empty.

But

Instances restricted to 133 certified optima from mixed-integer linear programming formulations. Annealer performance evaluated only on D-Wave hardware with 500 reads per configuration up to 1000 µs.

Tools

mixed Hamming packing formulation · MQLib feature analysis and heuristics · Simulated Bifurcation Machine (SBM) · Gurobi exact solver · D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer

Abstract

Benchmarking exact solvers and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) requires small yet challenging instances, preferably coming from actual applications. We propose such a benchmark set derived from mixed Hamming packing, a hard problem in coding theory. Starting from its mixed-integer linear programming formulation, we provide a generator for the equivalent QUBO models and study 133 instances whose optima are certified by that formulation. In the feature space of the MQLib library, we position a broad range of existing quantum-oriented benchmarks relative to the classical ones: they lie along a narrow, sparse border of the region covered by MQLib, whereas our instances form a coherent family in a region that both collections leave almost empty. Classical heuristics and a simulated bifurcation machine find the optimum of most instances quickly, in several cases sooner than an exact mixed-integer solver first encounters it, suggesting heuristic warm starts for exact solvers; for an exact QUBO solver, in turn, it appears challenging to prove optimality. In Ising form, the instances are densely connected antiferromagnets whose large local fields are almost exactly balanced by the couplings, so that the decision on each variable rests on a small remainder. This makes them hard to embed and to represent accurately on current quantum annealers, in line with our D-Wave experiments.
